It is not a hiring standard, ability score or assessment of job competence, nor does it constitute advice on nursing practice, medication administration, medical treatment, law or investment. This page corresponds to the specific US O*NET/SOC 31-1121.00 occupation, “Home Health Aides”: under the direction of offsite or intermittently onsite licensed nursing staff, they monitor the health of individuals with disabilities or illness and address health-related needs such as changing bandages, dressing wounds or administering medication, and assist with daily activities such as feeding, bathing, toileting or walking; depending on the patient’s abilities, they may also help prepare meals, do light housework and do laundry. Official scope, original wording: Monitor the health status of an individual with disabilities or illness, and address their health-related needs, such as changing bandages, dressing wounds, or administering medication. Work is performed under the direction of offsite or intermittent onsite licensed nursing staff. Provide assistance with routine healthcare tasks or activities of daily living, such as feeding, bathing, toileting, or ambulation. May also help with tasks such as preparing meals, doing light housekeeping, and doing laundry depending on the patient's abilities. US wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data and BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 as presented by O*NET; the page labels these figures as Home Health and Personal Care Aides (combined category). Exact occupational wage data for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. The two jurisdictions and their practice systems cannot be applied interchangeably.

To consider whether home health aide work suits you, first conduct a verifiable care exercise using public or simulated materials: choose a fictional service recipient (for example, an older adult with limited mobility who needs toileting assistance and medication reminders). Write a step-by-step process covering accepting the assignment and understanding the care plan, verifying identity and service scope, providing daily care (feeding, bathing, toileting, walking assistance and transfers), observing and recording health status, carrying out permitted care tasks as instructed by a supervisor or licensed nurse, and documenting and reporting at handover. Identify safety and scope checkpoints at each step and possible abnormalities (falls, damaged skin or pressure ulcers, choking during meals, fever or changes in consciousness, exposure to infection, refusal of care or agitation). Afterwards, check whether fall prevention, hand hygiene and infection protection are mandatory steps; whether medication administration, wound treatment, assessment of the patient’s condition and other matters beyond personal authorization are written as situations requiring you to stop and report to a licensed nurse or supervisor; and whether observed abnormalities are framed as actionable problems with records that can be reviewed. Test this through tangible deliverables rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | US O*NET 31-1121.00 work activity importance shows that providing personal assistance and care to others (95), obtaining information (87), communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates (86), and making decisions and solving problems (86) are the occupation’s most important activities. Work context shows: constant contact with others 79%; physical proximity 77% means very close; exposure to disease or infection 56% means daily; controlled indoor environments 62% means daily; importance of precision or accuracy 33% means extremely important and 35% very important; decision frequency 56% means daily; dealing with unpleasant, angry or rude people 46% means daily; face-to-face discussions 45% means daily; and typical workweek 53% means 40 hours. The most important skills are active listening (72), monitoring, reading comprehension, critical thinking and speaking; service orientation (75) and social perceptiveness (69) lead the transferable skills. If you are willing to provide close personal care over the long term under supervision, observe and truthfully record others’ physical condition, communicate patiently with patients and families, and follow procedures within infection and safety boundaries, these daily requirements are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (31-1121.00): constant contact with others 79%; physical proximity 77% means very close (nearly touching); exposure to disease or infection 56% means daily; dealing with unpleasant, angry or rude people 46% means daily; dealing with violent or physically aggressive people 38% means daily; high responsibility for others’ health and safety 23% and moderate responsibility 17%; repetitive motions 56% means continually or almost continually, standing 59% continually, and walking or running 56% continually. This occupation works with others’ bodies, health and emotions within a supervised care chain. A lapse in fall prevention, an omission in infection protection, dismissal of an observed abnormality, or an intervention beyond authorization may cause personal injury, exceed the scope of practice or produce inaccurate records. This page therefore separately addresses infection protection and safety, observation and records, authorization boundaries for medication administration and wound treatment, and patient information protection. In the US, the occupation is marked Bright Outlook. However, these wages and employment figures cover the combined Home Health and Personal Care Aides category, rather than the exact size of this occupation. If you find close personal care, infection exposure or prolonged interaction with emotionally unsettled people difficult to tolerate, treat these as practical costs to weigh carefully.

Judging responsibilities | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same shift: deliver care in practice (follow the care plan and instructions from a supervisor or licensed nurse to provide daily care such as feeding, bathing, toileting, walking assistance and transfers, producing care and observation records that can be reviewed); manage safety and scope (prevent falls and infection, perform permitted tasks as instructed, stop and report medication administration, wound treatment or other matters beyond personal authorization, protect patient information, and follow institutional and legal requirements); and take on defined role responsibilities (be accountable for your own care actions and truthful records, and refer judgments beyond your personal authority to a licensed nurse or supervisor). Use a verifiable experience, such as completing a step-by-step care process and observation record or practising recognition and handling of common care abnormalities, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire’s conclusions.

The daily work of home health aides can be divided into three streams: (1) care and assistance—helping with feeding, bathing, toileting, dressing, walking and transfers in people’s homes or care facilities, and doing housework related to personal care; (2) health monitoring and following instructions—checking pulse, temperature and breathing, observing and recording health status, and performing permitted care tasks under licensed nursing staff; (3) communication and records—recording observed conditions, progress or problems and reporting them to supervisors or case managers, while communicating with patients and families. These streams share safety and observation requirements but serve different recipients: care and monitoring serve the patient, while communication and records serve the care team and care logs.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 31-1121.00, this occupation monitors the health of individuals with disabilities or illness and addresses health-related needs (such as changing bandages, dressing wounds or administering medication) under offsite or intermittently onsite licensed nursing staff, and assists with daily activities such as feeding, bathing, toileting or walking. Typical tasks include planning, buying, preparing or serving meals according to prescribed diets (importance 91), caring for patients by changing bed linens and assisting with personal care (89), bathing patients (88), recording and reporting care conditions and progress (87), and helping patients into and out of beds, bathtubs, wheelchairs and cars and assisting dressing and grooming (84).
entries.question: What exactly do home health aides do?

entries.answer: Nursing aides and personal care aides also provide daily care but differ in authorization scope and regulation; occupational therapists and recreational therapists focus on therapeutic and activity-based interventions; registered nurses and acute care nurses assess patients’ conditions, make nursing diagnoses and provide independent treatment. Entry requirements, authorization scope and safety responsibilities differ; these occupations cannot be interchanged simply by job title.

subject.name: Home Health Aides
subject.summary: Home health aides correspond to the specific US O*NET/SOC 31-1121.00 occupation, “Home Health Aides”: under the direction of offsite or intermittently onsite licensed nursing staff, they monitor the health of individuals with disabilities or illness and address health-related needs (such as changing bandages, dressing wounds or administering medication), and assist with daily activities such as feeding, bathing, toileting or walking. Official scope, original wording: Monitor the health status of an individual with disabilities or illness, and address their health-related needs, such as changing bandages, dressing wounds, or administering medication. Work is performed under the direction of offsite or intermittent onsite licensed nursing staff. Provide assistance with routine healthcare tasks or activities of daily living, such as feeding, bathing, toileting, or ambulation. May also help with tasks such as preparing meals, doing light housekeeping, and doing laundry depending on the patient’s abilities. Core tasks include buying and preparing meals according to prescribed dietary plans (91), caring for patients (89), bathing patients (88), and recording and reporting care conditions (87). US wage and employment figures on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 as presented by O*NET; O*NET labels these wages and employment figures as the combined Home Health and Personal Care Aides category. Exact occupational wage data for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. Chinese boundaries for care practice and information protection are identified separately.
